t: Digit Count in Range — Counting Digits by Position
o: We must count occurrences of a single digit $d$ across every integer in [low, high], including repeated digits within one number (e.g. '11' contributes two 1s for d=1). In Example 1, the numbers 1, 10, 11, 12, 13 contain six 1s total (two from 11). In Example 2, scanning 100..250 yields 35 threes. Since high can be up to 2·10^8, iterating over every number and its ~9 digits is about 1.8·10^9 operations — too slow in Python and borderline elsewhere, so we need a mathematical/digit-DP style solution that runs in time proportional to the number of digits.
k: Count(d in [low, high]) = count(d in [1, high]) - count(d in [1, low-1]); solve only the prefix-counting problem.
For each digit position of n, count how many numbers ≤ n have digit d at that position by splitting n into high/mid/low parts around that position.
The formula differs for d = 0 because leading zeros are not written; handle it with an extra condition on the high part.

a.i: Simply iterate over every integer in [low, high] and count occurrences of d in its decimal representation. This directly mirrors the problem statement and is trivially correct, but with up to 2·10^8 numbers of up to 9 digits each it is far too slow for the given constraints — included mainly as a correctness baseline.
s: For each number x from low to high, convert x to a string.
Add the number of characters equal to str(d) to the answer.
a.t: O((high - low + 1) · log(high)) — each number has at most 9 digits; roughly 10^9 operations at max constraints.

a.i: Define f(n, d) = number of times d appears in all integers from 1 to n; the answer is f(high) − f(low−1). To compute f(n, d), consider each digit position p (units, tens, ...) independently: write n's digits around position p as high | cur | low, where cur is the digit at p and pow is 10^p. The count of numbers ≤ n having digit d at position p is: if cur > d, (high+1)·pow; if cur == d, high·pow + low + 1; if cur < d, high·pow. For d = 0 subtract pow when high > 0, since numbers cannot have a leading zero at that position. Summing over positions gives f(n, d) in O(log n).
s: Implement count(n, d): if n <= 0 return 0.
Iterate positions with pow = 1 while pow <= n; extract high = n // (pow * 10), cur = (n // pow) % 10, low = n % pow.
If cur > d add (high + 1) * pow; if cur == d add high * pow + low + 1; else add high * pow.
If d == 0 and high > 0, subtract pow (no leading zeros).
a.t: O(log(high)) — one pass over the ~9 digit positions of n, done twice (for high and low−1).
a.sp: O(1) — only a few scalar variables.

w: In an interview, mention brute force briefly to show you understand the problem, then present the per-position counting approach as the real solution — it is the standard technique behind LeetCode 233 (Number of Digit One) generalized to any digit d. Key pitfalls: forgetting the low−1 boundary (use long arithmetic so low−1 = 0 works), mishandling d = 0 due to leading zeros, and integer overflow in C++/Java when computing pw*10 or (hi+1)*pw near 2·10^8 (fits in long long / long). Edge cases to test: d = 0, low = high, low = 1, and ranges containing repdigits like 111. Likely follow-ups: extend to counting a multi-digit pattern, or count digits in [low, high] for all ten digits at once (same loop, no extra asymptotic cost).
